reference.source: Miller's Review of Orthopaedics / Brukner and Khan's Clinical Sports Medicine
clinicalPearls: A small avulsion fracture off the lateral margin of the proximal tibia, just distal to the joint line
It results from internal rotation and varus stress and represents avulsion of the anterolateral capsuloligamentous complex
Its great importance is as a radiographic marker: it is strongly associated with (nearly pathognomonic of) anterior cruciate ligament rupture
It is frequently accompanied by meniscal injury as well as the ACL tear
A reverse Segond (medial tibial rim avulsion) is instead associated with PCL and medial meniscal injury
The fleck of bone can be subtle on radiographs, so its recognition should trigger MRI of the knee
Treatment is directed at the associated intra-articular injuries rather than the small bony fragment itself
reference.pathophysiology: Excessive internal rotation and varus loading of the knee places tension on the anterolateral structures of the proximal tibia, avulsing a small cortical fragment at their insertion. The same mechanism ruptures the anterior cruciate ligament, which is why the Segond fragment is a reliable secondary sign of ACL injury; the bony fragment itself is usually clinically insignificant compared with the associated ligamentous and meniscal damage.
additionalDifferentials: Arcuate (fibular head avulsion) fracture indicating posterolateral corner injury
Reverse Segond (medial avulsion) with PCL injury
Iliotibial band or biceps femoris avulsion
additionalInvestigations: Radiographs of the knee (the fragment is best seen on the AP view)
MRI to confirm ACL rupture and detect meniscal injury
Lachman and pivot-shift examination for anterior instability
Assessment for associated posterolateral corner injury
redFlags: Multiligament injury or a reduced knee dislocation with vascular risk
Locked knee suggesting a displaced meniscal fragment
Gross rotatory instability implying posterolateral corner involvement
reference.prognosis: The fracture itself heals without specific treatment; the outcome is determined by the associated ACL and meniscal injuries and their management.
pitfalls: Overlooking the subtle bony fleck and thereby missing the associated ACL rupture
Treating the fragment in isolation while ignoring intra-articular injury
Confusing it with an arcuate fracture that signals posterolateral corner injury
Failing to obtain MRI after identifying the sign
references: Rockwood and Green's Fractures in Adults
management: Recognise the fragment as a marker of anterior cruciate ligament rupture and image the knee with MRI to define the ligamentous and meniscal injury
Manage the bony avulsion itself non-operatively, as it heals without specific fixation
Provide initial symptomatic care with rest, ice, analgesia and bracing or protected weight-bearing
Treat the associated ACL rupture with reconstruction in active or unstable patients, or with rehabilitation in lower-demand patients
Address concurrent meniscal or posterolateral corner injury surgically as indicated
Undertake structured physiotherapy and graded return to activity, with orthopaedic and sports medicine follow-up
